TOOTS THIELEMANS
NEA Jazz Master (2009)
Interviewee: Toots Thielemans (April 29, 1922 – August 22, 2016)
Interviewer: Anthony Brown with recording engineer Ken Kimery Date: August 31 and September 1, 2011 Description: Transcript, 80 pp.

Today is August 31, 2011. My name is Anthony Brown, and I am conducting the Smithsonian Institution Oral History with NEA Jazz Master, harmonica virtuoso, guitarist and whistler, Toots Thielemans. Hello…
Yes, my real name is Jean.
Jean.
And in Belgium… I was born in Belgium. Jean-Baptiste Frédéric Isidor. Four first names. And then Thielemans.
That’s funny.
And in French-speaking Belgium, they will pronounce it Thielemans. But I was born April 29, 1922.
That’s Duke Ellington’s birthday, as well.
Yes.
All right.
Yes, same day.
Yeah, same day. Just a few years later. [laughs]
[laughs] Oh, Duke. Okay.
Where in Belgium? What city?
In Brussels.
That’s the capitol.

In a popular neighborhood of Brussels called Les Marolles. There was… I don’t know, I wouldn’t know which neighborhood to equivalent in New York. Would that be Lower East Side? Or whatever… popular. And my folks, my father and mother, were operating, so to speak, a little beer café—no alcohol but beer, and different beers—in this café on High Street, Rue Haute, on the Marolles. And then the little café was called the Kop Knuff [?]—the Little Step Down. That’s Flemish. And that’s it. [laughs]
And your parents’ names.

My father was Bernard Thielemans, and my mother was Egmas [?] [unintelligible]. Don’t try to spell it. [laughs] She was from Antwerp. My father was from Brussels. And there were some roots from Walloon, from the mine work. This province in Wallonia, and my uncles were mine workers. So there’s a total scope, total mixture of Belgian, Flemish, Walloon French, and Brussels. That’s so I’m three linguist to start.
So Flemish, French, and English or…
No, not yet.
French and…

But later on, when I start to travel. But in school, in those days when you went to école moyenne, they called it. It takes twelve years. You have six years elementary and then six years secondary, right? And my direction was mathematics and languages. So at age… after twelve years of school, I could speak… We had good English teachers, good German. So the four languages were French, Flemish, English, and German. So when I was sixteen, I could write business letters in English and in German. And of course, by then, the movies, you know… James Cagney and all those. So I learned English, you know, real quick.
Could you talk about your parents? What were their jobs or occupations?
Occupation? They tried to operate that café, and my mother, you know, we had a sister was born, too. She’s still alive—Mariette.
Younger sister?

Younger sister. Six, seven years. She was born in ’29, and I was born in ’22. And now we Skype, you know. We have a ball. [laughs] And so, and they were just… there was enough work to do with operating that little Kop Knuff [?]. [laughs]
Okay.
Thank you, Anthony.
Oh, Toots, it’s a pleasure. Let’s talk a little bit about your childhood. Maybe your neighborhood. Was there music in the neighborhood? Were there kinds of entertainment? Circus?
Yes.
Anything to captivate your imagination.

Well, there was a popular neighborhood in those days, and this neighborhood has changed considerably. But this is when I was three years old. Little Jean. Jean, that’s me playing the accordion. And in Brussels, I could show it to you. We still have the accordion. And on that, when I was three years old, my mother took me to the movie to see a film of Ramón Novarro. That was the big love symbol. But that song Ramóna… [plays tune on harmonica and sings] “Ramóna.” And then when I came home from the movie, I was… So I scared everybody. This little kid…
[laughs]

And then my father being a Socialist, you know… militant fighting. They were still fighting for the fifty-hour week, you know. Really progressive. I mean, there were no progressing. [laughs] And uh, so I played this was in then… [singing] “C’est la vie [ta finale?].” [plays tune] You know, the Socialist things. And here there’s some popular Brussels with lyrics—unprintable lyrics. [laughs]
So why did you play accordion?

I didn’t know why. I forget. Oh. Thanks for the question. Uh… I was sitting in, you call it, my crib or what it was. And every Sunday in the café, the [Kop Knuff?], there was an accordion player. And he put his hat on the floor, and he was playing, you know. And I was

imitating his motions with the accordion, but I took it… I did it with a shoebox. You know, they still have those cardboard shoeboxes, right? And that was the… that, I guess, my father… And one of the [unintelligible], they call him—one of the customers of the [Kop Knuff?]—said… Can I say it in Flemish?
Yes.

Typical Brussels dialect. [unintelligible; in Flemish] “It looks like this little one wants to play the accordion.” And then my father… first the cardboard. This is the second one. After I got good on the first cardboard, this is a graduation. [laughs]
So this picture you were how old?
How old am I? You can judge. I don’t know. Three, four? I don’t know.
[laughs] So you learned how to walk, talk, and then play accordion?
Yeah. I guess so. [laughs]
That’s amazing. So in school, was there music in the schools?
No.
Were you encouraged to be… No?

No. We had one hour a week solfeggio, you know. But no, the music was forgotten, you know. I was a good student in a weak class. [laughs] I was the most, if not first, you know. And my… later on when I was fifteen, I had to make decisions where I am going to go in the university. And mathematics was the choice. But music started to take over, of course. We had all the phonographs, you know, where you put the needle and you have two place with that needle. And then you have to wind up the phonograph again. And that’s much later. Oh, my God. My first Louis Armstrong record. We were living in a suburb of Brussels, of course. And around about 100 yards walk from where… that was during the German occupation already, you know, 1940. And this lady said, in the record store—78s, of course. No CD or no digital. And this lady said, “Jean,” lets me in. No [inaudible]. [laughs] [in French] “Jean, tu doit acheter ce disque.” “You must buy this record.” “C’est Louis Armstrong avec les Mills Brothers.” That’s French speaking, you know. Louis Armstrong and the Mills Brothers. And we played that, and we still have that wind-up phonograph, you know. And I remember, Louis Armstrong’s trumpet exploded so clear on the loudspeaker on the phonograph. And that was… And then when I was about twelve, thirteen, fourteen, we lived in Brussels but… and near where we lived, there was a cinema, movie houses, right? And every Wednesday or Thursday—I’ve forgotten now—for one franc… I don’t know how much that would be today. One Belgian franc… six, seventy years ago, we could go matinee movies—all the American—James Cagney, you know, of those eras. And one of the movies showed, in one of the movies there was a scene where one of the prisoners was waiting for his turn to go and be in electric chair. [laughs] And he was playing the harmonic. [singing] I said, “Hey, that’s nice. I’m gonna buy one.” [laughs]

That’s how it started. No, a real simple one yet, you know. This is a chromatic one, not the diatonic. And that’s it. And that started to… And after I was, of course, contaminated by Louis Armstrong, you know, I started to listen. That was still before liberation, you know. That was… the Germans were occupying and they were not encouraging music by colored people or Jewish people, you know. Benny Goodman, for instance. But we had, anyway, we had friends who had… There’s always been a subculture or underground group of musicians or jazz fans in Belgium. Even in Germany, I’m sure there was under Hitler. And so I bought the Django Reinhardt. No, the musicians started to say, they started to hear me show musicianship with this, you know. And then they said, “Jean, throw that toy away, you know. Get a real instrument.” Sure, you know, okay, here I am. And on a bet… So, to show you everything that happened to me happened to me. I never looked for trying to get anything or submit. “No, sir, I can do that if you want.” No, no. So I had a friend during the War occupation, whose uncle sold liquor in the black market. And he has… Gilbert. He’s still alive, I hope, in California. And he received money for his uncle, had a lot of money, and every week he bought an instrument until he found out, of course, it takes… He had two lessons on the drums and he [inaudible], you know. And that was his week for guitar. [laughs] Believe it or not, Gilbert. And we were already friends. We fooled around with the harmonicas—a little group and [stuff?]. And I was in bed. I had pneumonia. I was really in bad shape. But Gilbert came to visit me at where we lived in my parents, and with a guitar under his arm. And I asked, I said, “What you doing with this guitar?” “Ah, I’m disgusted. I came from the teacher, and I…” [laughs] But you know, the beautiful part of this… he tried to play the Fats Waller song. [singing] “Hold tight, hold…” On one string, you know. “Hold tight, hold tight fododo-de-yacka saki. Want some seafood.” You know this?
Mm-hmm.

Well, that’s… We all knew that, you know. All the little jazz fans that we were. We knew that and we knew Boogie Boogie or whatever was… But [unintelligible] Fats Waller. And then I said, “Gilbert…” I had already notions of solfeggio but not so much. “I can play that song on one string on your guitar in five minutes.” And I took… And that’s a typical blues phrase. [plays phrase, then sings] “Fododo-de-yacka saki. Want some seafood…mama. Shrimpers and rice, they’re really nice…” You know, that’s Fats Waller. And I said, “Gilbert, je sais jouer song en dix minutes.” [inaudible] And I was sick in bed. And he gave me the guitar. He said, “Eh…” He was… So that was how I became a guitar player. [laughs] So it was all planned, right? [laughs] And then, then I started to buy the Django Reinhardt records. We still found [inaudible], you know. And there were still other records, you know. We got every… We had access to every record that could come from the States, for instance, before liberation. As long as the Germans occupied Belgium, we lost all possibility to get records from America, for instance, you know. So, but there was a lot. There was a lot of the Jimmie Lunceford. [singing] “Four or five times…” And all those songs. [singing] “And the flat foot floogie with a floy…” [laughs] All those songs we… And that was the… I mean, my… almost you can start to call it maybe my soul contamination. [laughs] Yes, [alchemy?].
Oh, that’s great. Well, you say contamination. It sounds more like celebration. It made you happy this music, yes?

Yes, but I call… lately, I’ve been calling jazz a virus. And when the room is occupied… the spectators, the people who come to listen to see a [inaudible] concert, you will be contaminated yourself if you are here. If you were not, your contamination makes you a jazz fan. Something like that.
Uh-huh.
And it’s true.
Yeah. But it’s a positive contamination, yes? [laughs]
Yeah. It’s a good virus. [laughs] It’s positive but it’s a good one. [laughs]
Uh-huh. So were you able to get into music groups where you were playing jazz?

During the War, you know, a little bit. And then I became… quickly I became a good guitar player. Studying from those records of Django. Django was a fantastic… The records of Django Reinhardt were fantastic. Well, I never got that velocity, you know. He was… But uh… see, the harmonica, as fantastic as it is, you can only play one note. [plays scales on harmonica] And with the guitar you can play chords. And then I started to study harmony, you know. You could know… you’d follow a C major. C7 goes usually to F. That sort of thing. And then the guitar, of course… I had put… in the meantime, I gave up my… I flopped, flunked at the university… royally. [laughs] No, but it was… And my bad, poor health, you know. So I became a decent guitar player, I guess. And I learned a lot. And after the liberation, you know, the one record I was totally… I saw the guitar players of my generation in Europe outside of the States were Django-influenced very muchly. And but, I wanted more than… Django’s music is a branch of jazz, so to speak, but the three of jazz’s mainstream… not to call it mainstream, but the African American music—Ellington and Armstrong, Count Basie and all that, you know. And… [laughs] So… Oh, after liberation, I played even during the German offensive in the Ardennes, you know, where we were almost divided, you know, the… it was lucky that the American troops and Allied troops were able to keep the Germans where they should be. [laughs] And so I was playing in some café, jazz, with the guitar, and there was one cold winter where I played the guitar with my gloves. [laughs] And we received all and was hanging out in the GI clubs and the officer clubs in American troops. And we found what the American troops received was the hit kits, that was songs. [singing] “I walk alone.” All the songs of the War, you know. [singing] “I wish I knew…” And so I learned all those songs, you know, and we played them for the soldiers who came for, on their permission. You know, they had two, three days off and they went to Brussels to… [laughs] to live a little bit, you know. And that’s how I started to play, you know, with a pianist and bass and the drum and me. No harmonica. Nobody wanted to hear that, you know. [laughs]
So Toots, when you say you were ill, what disease did you have?

Asthma and pneumonia. And I still have to be careful for asthma. In my life, I went through the total scope of asthma puffs and even… oh, that’s a beautiful anecdote. Even when I came to the States the first time. That was in ’47, with my uncle, the brother of my father. And we went… There was a club—The Embers. I wound up playing there with the George Shearing Quartet. And I went to listen. I knew all the records. I was up on all my bebop. And in the Embers restaurant, jazz place, there was the trio with Red Norvo, the vibraphonist, with Tal Farlow, fantastic guitar player that was [interested in me?]. And Charlie Mingus played bass with that trio.
Right.

And I went there, and I went in the dressing room, met the guy, and I took something out of my pocket. They was passing a cigarette. And I… and that smelled just like marijuana. And all the guys were, “Hey, man, [unintelligible], too, you know [what I mean?]?” [laughs] That’s a beautiful anecdote. And then they… the medicine graduated, so to speak, from a cigarette to a puff first [for one of those?]. And now they have absolutely perfect for my kind of asthma. My kind of asthma. [laughs] So that’s another good… You’ll have to clip a lot.
Yeah, it’s okay. Let’s go back before you made your first trip to America. So the occupation ended. So you flunked out of the university. So you really are now going…
Yeah.
Not going to be a mathematician. You’re going to be a musician. Is this what’s in your mind?

Yes. Yes. And I’m… I played but we [inaudible]. I have to do [inaudible] for quite a few years. Play the melody for the people who want to dance so whatever, you know. And but I listened to all the records. I was totally acquainted, you know, the Dizzy Gillespie records and Charlie Parker, you know. I’m talking now about ’45, 6, 7.
Right.

And we had friends, sailors, who went back and forth between America, and we bought all of the records. One bass Hit, the big orchestra with Dizzy. And the big orchestra and the small orchestra. And all the Charlie Parker. And there was… that bebop, you know, explosion was something… I expected many of the musicians of my generation were waiting for something like that to happen in jazz. And that was one of the first hurdles, really. The evolution of jazz started with, [you’d say?], King Oliver and Louie Armstrong and then the people like Eddie Lang, Joe Venuti, [inaudible] and [inaudible]. And the swing bands. And then there was that hurdle—bebop, you know. And many of the guys who could play perfect swing

music were not able, and I was fortunate. I guess I had… I was right away a bebopper, you know. I mean, I was… I can say I was. And then I kept studying, and I finally got my… I played for the Belgian Jazz Club, Jazz Federation as a trio when we went to Paris for the jazz festival.
What year?
That was 1949.
Oh, that’s when Charlie Parker was there. And Miles Davis.
Yeah. Oh, yeah.
With Tadd Dameron.

And as it was, I had made… I came to the States in ’47 with my uncle, and I met Hank Jones and those guys at 52nd Street. That was the Three Deuces. And every week there was an all-star group but with the same guys. One week was J.J. Johnson, the leader. One week was Howard McGee, a fine trumpet player. And we went there. Now it’s getting long. I have to talk about maybe, I was in Miami with my uncle for his vacation. I went with him to Miami.
This is still in 1947? That same trip?

Yeah, yeah. Thank you. And in Miami, that was the period of the Nat King Cole popularity. [singing] “Straighten up and fly right.” [unintelligible], you know. And in every restaurant, there was a trio—bass, piano, and guitar. And one of the guys sang. [laughs] You know, all of them are singing. And I went to one of those restaurants, and I became, you know, when a musician meets a musician, after two minutes, after the first word, you know—oh, this guy knows his stuff. I’ll stay here and talk to him. You know? And I became friends with the guitar player. “Yeah, I play the guitar myself but I prefer blah blah.” And I said, “And I play that.” “Oh yeah?” You know? And I sat in with the band. And who was in that restaurant that night was Bill Gottlieb. That’s the photographer. And he, you know, he was the photographer of the music, you know. And he said, “Hey, you’re good, man. What’s happening?” Well, I have to go… I’m here with my uncle, but I have to go back via New York, where I can get on the boat in New York to go to Genoa and to play with the Belgian guys at the Nice Jazz Festival. “Well, if you come to New York, call me. I’ll take you to the Street.” [That would be?] [inaudible] at 52nd Street, of course. And then he took me to the Street, and there was just Hank Jones, for instance, and all those guys—Percy Heath, Jimmie Heath, probably, and J.J. Something like that. And he said, “What do you want to play [inaudible]?” So Bill Gottlieb goes to the guy. “Hey guy, guys, I’ve got a great guy here from Belgium.” “Boo, Belgium. Where’s that?” You know? “And he plays the harmonica.” “Boo!” No, I’m making it… But it was… the feeling was about like that. They didn’t expect. And Hank, [inaudible] Hank. I knew of Hank. I had his records. Yeah, we knew. I had all the records. He was before ’47, you know. And uh, “Oh, Mr. Jones.” “What do you want to play?” And then, it was, I can’t get started. And the second and the third or fourth bar was a chromatic sequence that if you could master that, that opened the door for bebop, you were an acceptable bebopper. That’s it. [plays harmonica] And now.

[plays a few more bars] But I play it a little better now, I hope. [laughs] But the whole band, “Wow.” No, this was like chromatic, minor 7, 7th, B minor 7th, E7, then B-flat, you know. And that was a fantastic exercise besides. And I [inaudible]. And “Hey, hey.” And I stayed two days. I sat at the piano and I had my guitar, too. “I’ll bring it tomorrow.” [laughs] There was Three Deuces. And then… [laughs] “This is beautiful. Thank you.” And one of those nights… You know, I was there two nights. The other group was Lennie Tristano. I sat in with them. [I?] didn’t move from the piano. I had a high stool, a bar stool, so to speak. And they just came by— Billy Shaw. And Billy Shaw was, you know, the salesman of… the representative to be respected. The representative of bebop—Charlie Parker and [later on?] Miles, and [inaudible]. And, “Where are you from?” You know? In typical Hollywood, you know. “Where are you from?” “I’m from Brussels.” “Oh, I know. That’s in Copenhagen.” [laughs] I swear to you. It’s just… “Send me records.” Just say, “Yes. Yes, sir.” “I’ll make you the Belgian king of bebop.” That really shocked me. I remember… I swear. Why would I lie sixty years later? [laughs] And uh, that’s happened.
So…
That was the… oh, I got some sort of a door, a little toe in the jazz door in New York.
Well, it sounds like you made quite a splash ‘cause… [laughs]

Yeah, with this, you know. I was showing that I was totally up-to-date in my.... If you can play that [fluid?] and with musical sense, those three, two bars… [plays harmonica] Half a step, [inaudible] half a step. [plays one bar] But that’s just the main notes used, but then you can… [plays a couple more bars] You know, all that you can do.
You’re playing more than one note at a time now. [laughs]
Well, they go so fast it sounds like that. [laughs]
What month were you there? So it was 1947 and you’re in New York. You’re at the Three Deuces. Do you remember at least the season? Was it spring, summer, fall, winter?
It must, must have been… because… excuse me… the festival in Nice, where I had to join the Belgian delegation… [laughs] And that was… it must have been something like February or something.
So in the winter, you were in New York.
Yeah.
Not autumn in New York. You’re winter in New York.
Maybe. But I didn’t… there was no snow that I remember.
Okay, okay. So you have expansive harmonic knowledge by the time you’re playing bebop.
Yes.
Is this all self-taught, or did you have somebody help you, or was this like musicians…?

No, the… Well, I learned on the spot, you know, and whenever I’d see another [good reader?]. And the records were enough for me. If you can play all the bebop runs, you know, and apply them. Not just play, be a clone. That’s what I always try to, even now, especially now.
And had you played or seen any American musicians before you came to America? Did they come to Brussels or to Belgium?
Not yet. But there was one… Good question. Redmond.
Don Redman? No.
Big orchestra.
Yeah, Don Redman. He was…
Don Redman.
Yeah. He used to be…

And in that orchestra, there was Don Byas. We became good friends through [unintelligible]. I still remember the way he played the melody. Don Byas. Peanuts Holland was the trumpet [player?]. He stayed in Denmark. Many of the guys… a couple of the guys… and Billy Taylor was the young pianist. And of course, always he was very hospitable to me when I came to the States in ’51.
So winter of ’47, your first trip to America. You go back. You join up with your Belgian delegation to perform in Nice.
In Nice, yeah.
And…

There was just… We weren’t that [unintelligible] as a group. [laughs] But there were good musicians. There was a saxophonist—Bobby Jaspar, and he played… he wound up playing. He came here and played a lot.
Oh, yeah.
In his fifties. Oh, I have an anecdote.
Go ahead.
May I?
Sure. [laughs]

Because Bobby Jaspar, the saxophone player, very talented, played with J.J. Johnson in the ’50s—’54 or 5, around there. And I was with Shearing, and we played the same circuit, you know. And outside of Detroit, there’s a town, a factory, car factory—River Rouge. Do they still exist? [inaudible]
Probably not. [laughs]

No, the thing is, a town where they only make cars, you know. I mean, they make a lot of cars. And in that River Rouge, there was a jazz club—The Rouge Lounge, or something. And we played there. [laughs] We checked in with George, you know, and I brought my guitar and my amplifier, and we do a sound check. And then I go to the men’s room. I’ll tell you. And I go pee, and I say, in French, “Toots [inaudible].” Toots has a big dick. [laughs] And I say that in French in River Rouge. How do they know? [laughs] First of all, it’s not true. [laughs] But that’s the sense of humor from Bobby Jaspar. He played there the week before with J.J. Johnson, you know. Toots… [laughs] See, those kind of anecdotes, they make a lot of sense and they’re connected to the music, you know. [laughs]
Who else was in the Belgian, your group? Bobby Jasper, yourself.

And a good vibraphone player. He died. Uh… [Savie Larlamans?]. And he was really Hampton, a little more articulate harmonically. But he was a showman and a combination Fats Waller and Lionel Hampton, you know.
Whoo. [laughs]

But he had this place he played a lot in Paris, but he never really came to the States. Then that was [inaudible]. Oh, and Jacques [Belzer?], the alto player who played a lot later on with Chet Baker.
So two saxophone, vibes, and guitar, harmonica?
There was a pianist, I forgot. No, not so, not so easy to remember. [laughs]
But bass or drums? No?
Yeah, there was a bass.
So it was a pretty big group.
Yeah, it was a quintet, you know, but…
Okay.
We didn’t really break it up. [laughs] And that’s when Louie Armstrong… I did that was… I didn’t go over to shake hands. That happened later.
Oh, okay.
When I was with Shearing. [laughs]
So, but in ’49, you went to the Paris Jazz Festival. And like I said…
And like I said, they had a lot of Americans there.
Yeah.
Bird and Miles.
Oh. I remember when Miles was there with Kenny Clark, [I think?].
Tadd Dameron. Pierre Michelot.
No, he didn’t [unintelligible/overlapping].
Yeah, well…
But he had Miles, anyway. His sound, you know… I wasn’t, of course
[unintelligible/overlapping voices].
And they had James Moody. Miles and James Moody and Tadd Dameron.
[overlapping voices] Oh, yeah. Yeah, and…
And Kenny Clark.
[unintelligible] Kenny Dorham.
Mm-hmm. And Max.

And Max, yeah. Yeah, you’re right, my friend. It happens so often that you get involved in interviews, where the guy who asks the questions don’t know what you’re talking about or has no reference to the subject, you know. And then, you spoil me. You’re gonna make it hard for all… [laughs] …who follow me, interviewers. No. No, this is just a person appreciates [inaudible], you know. But where were we?
Talking about the…
Oh, the Paris festival.
Yeah. This is a big festival.

But then, in those days, there still was the War. In French, I would say, “La guerre [in French].” “The war of the ancient, the old jazz and the newer jazz.” The old jazz was sort of pioneer defended by politically… not politically, but it sounded like a political opposition. [Parnacier?]. [in French] [unintelligible] [Parnacier?]. It was [inaudible] or you might could say Armstrong. Armstrong was almost too modern for him, you know. [inaudible] just about. It was more to [unintelligible], you know those things? I respect that. But then there was the newer word—[in French]—the right of poet. I never… I shook hands with him once but I never… I never was enough in Paris to meet him. Anyway, so that’s it. You were on a good question.
Well, yeah, because…

In, in Paris, I didn’t… I shook hands and… We were blown away because the harmonica, you know. It was years. They still call it the miscellaneous instrument. But then they didn’t. That’s a piece of, you know what, you know. And so they booed me. Then in the second, I had… and they laughed, also, because when I speak French, I had… then, they’d be a little less now maybe… but a typical Belgian accent. And the French liked to make fun of the Belgian accent, also. But you know… But when I played the guitar, I was accepted.
Can we go… talk about this, about the unacceptance of Belgian culture and French. What is the history of that?
No, it’s not culture. It’s…
Just that language?
That’s just the language.
Okay.

No. There is… Belgian who tried to speak French [inaudible]. There’s a lot of Belgian literature, you know, and literary people accept it. No, that was typical. The slang of Brussels that they… of Belgian, also. No, that has nothing to do with music.
Okay. But it was just a language…
Yeah, just a joke.
And maybe the French, they want everything exactly like French? No? [laughs]
No. It was not that.
Okay.
No. It was [dual?]. If a French guy played modern jazz, he was also getting booed. [laughs] You know what I mean? Yeah, it was not just because Belgian.
Okay. But for me, or for you…

Yeah, yeah. So… let me see. No, here… No, the year is actually 2009, so this is wrong. George Benson, Jimmy Cobb…
Yeah.
Lee Konitz, Rudy Van Gelder, Snooky Young. Snooky. [laughs]
Yeah. [inaudible/overlapping voices]
Yeah. Yeah, so 2009 was the year.
But I think Snooky was not somebody… two other guys came. Frank West and the California band leader.
Gerald Wilson.
Gerald Wilson talked about the achievements of Snooky, who was sitting, you know. I remember that.
Who introduced you or talked on your behalf?
Billy Taylor.
Ah. [laughs]
Billy Taylor. Dr. Billy Taylor. He died, also. He was very hospitable to me when I came… As I told you, we played with the Don Redmond Band.
Right, you did.

Touring Europe. And that’s where… dressed like that, but [inaudible], “Hey, this guy can play,” you know, that sort of thing, before I came to the States. And then, when I just had my permits but I didn’t have the union permit. I had to be six months of a resident, proved residence in New York to be able to work. And Billy was playing the piano at the Hickory House. There was a piano. [Marian McPartland?], [Bac Bachman?] played there, also. And I was, I had a job for a couple of months waiting for me card at [Spina?] Airlines, [inaudible] Airlines. I made… I won’t say [inaudible] much, but it wasn’t much. But at least I wasn’t starving, you know, with my wife. And so, he let me… I could… I had enough money maybe to go for one beer at Hickory House on the weekends, you know. And Billy invited me to play. And he remembered that when he gave me the award, the diploma, I think it was… Yes, he wasn’t… Yeah, but… [laughs]
So…
Some people… sometimes I say I’m grateful that I’m still here to talk about all that. [laughs]
No, we’re grateful, too. [laughs]
Yeah.
Let’s talk a little about… because I saw in 2007, you performed a jazz master class series in NYU. So let’s talk about teaching. How do you teach this music? What do you… what is important?

I have found out I cannot teach, but what I can do… I can show my, what I learned, what I use for practice. It’s enough on a small piece of paper that what I need, need, is to be able to play the chords and formal scales in the C major. [plays C major scale] C minor [plays scale] Or… [plays] And then the diminished. And then the altered chords. [plays scales] That’s… oh, it’s my loved... my beloved C altered going to F. [plays scales] You know? [plays scale] That’s F to [inaudible]. That’s a C-7th with a F-sharp feeling. [plays scales] You know? Things like that. And that’s what you have to know in every key then, when… you know. And that’s enough to… it’s just three scales that you have to know [inaudible]. You know? From one to the other. In every key. And look on the harmonica or whatever instrument you play, the runs that lay easy. For instance, C-7th… G-7th. [plays scales] You know, that… that’s only G-7th, of course. You know? [laughs] Don’t laugh. It’s true. That’s what it is. And

then, you have to be able to play that stuff in F-sharp, also, not just in G. And in E-flat. E-flat. [plays scales] That’s also E-flat 7th. When A combined with A altered, whatever. I don’t know even the names of those things, you know. I wouldn’t know how to… but I have them here, and I hear them.
Well, we were talking yesterday that, you know…

That, that’s… but in terms of teaching, I can tell the guy the names of the scales and the notes that go into it, you know. But not… an instrument is a person, you know. No teaching and… I, when I play something, if you ask me, “Hey, sir, what do you call what you just played?” That I [can?] explain. And then try to do that in that key played slower, of course, if you want. But take it part by part and then… Then you go into every key and [inaudible] you do that shit in every key, you’re [inaudible]. [laughs] But then, the guys today, they… the pentatonic, you know, or the blue notes, you know. It’s… [plays] Oh-ho-ho-ho, mama. [laughs] Did you hear?
Yeah. I heard a little straight note chasing and then it went way out. [laughs]

You know, that… see, and… you have to… the whole thing is to tell the story with taste, you know. It’s not about how many notes you can play. It’s how many right notes and tasteful, and that’s, that’s where the meditation comes in, I guess. Or listen, listen to yourself. For instance, that thing I played for you, I can’t play it anymore today that… [sings] That’s too fast. But those runs I do, won’t play them, either anymore. That’s thirty years ago, you know. Even though they still hold up. Of course, they will. But I would say I trimmed my tree. If you [call me?], your language. If you improvise, it’s your language, right? And that language becomes a tree. When you become… And after thirty years, that tree… some of those branches are getting tired or worn out or you don’t want to hear them anymore, so you’ve got to trim the tree. That’s what… In French, they would say, “[elongé”?]—trim the tree—elongé.” In Flemish, how do they say it?
[Snuya?].
Huh?
[Snuya?]
[Snuya?] [speaks in Flemish] [unintelligible] [snuya?]. The tree bomb. Not bomb, bomb.
Bomb.
You little tree, [snuya?], please. He went to school in Flemish, too, you know. [laughs] Thank you for everything.
Say your name for the tape?
Peter [Lombart?].
Oh, great. Okay.

So, that’s it. That’s what I… I’m into now. I’m always being into. Even… but now, I try to say this as much with fewer notes. Is it Miles who said, “Less is more”? Something like that. And okay, just listen. Keep listen. Keep listening. I listen to… for instance, this lady, Terri Lyne Carrington. Isn’t she [mean?] [inaudible]. I think she’s mean, you know.
Yeah.

And I think these days, she’s companion… she has a companion, Greg Osby. They’re together. This… that’s a little… Greg Osby or Steve Coleman. The sound remains… their touch and their tone production is, without a doubt is from your side of the street. [laughs] But somehow the blue note… you know, I’m old-fashioned. I mean that… [plays harmonica] Well, I’m exaggerating now, you know. And [inaudible]… [plays] You know? But day to day, they can do that. But they… somehow their runs I don’t always… but more power to them, you know. Who am I, you know?
Are there any youngsters that catch your ear? Anybody playing from the younger generation that you..
I listen to them, and there’s a few trumpet players. [Patch?] something. And a guitar player. I have him there. [inaudible] And this Indian fellow… Eli [Jai?]…
Oh. Vijay Iyer. He’s a piano player. And then Rudresh Mahanthappa.
Yeah.
A saxophone player.
Yeah. And oh. The tenor playing with him, I like. Rudish…
Yeah, Rudresh.
Ooo. [laughs]
He’s mixing the Indian.
And he sounds like… he’s a singer, a religious singer of this country. [imitates] I beg your pardon. But he sounds… that’s it. I have it here and everything. I listen to those cats.

And here and there, something’s [inaudible]. I’m not, I’m not, I would say, this… I’m still [rubbable?]. [laughs] I’m still a, you know, it’s not [that I’m just standstill?]. There’s still a little balls here and there for some of that shit. [laughs]
[laughs] That’s great. Keep an open mind, right?
Yeah. [inaudible/overlapping voices]
Keep open mind, open heart.
That’s right.
Mm-hmm. Do you have any projects that you want to do?
Any what?
Any projects or any…

No, we do. For instance, we have… I have some great musicians I [inaudible]. We’re doing some jobs, you know, with some European rhythm section. They’re good. Then we… but I like to play what… okay, I [would?] start my set with Dave Brubeck. The… Your Sweet, you know.
In Your Own Sweet Way.

Sweet, yeah. You know. [plays a few bars] And then, on the second after that, I would play My Wine and Roses. [plays a few bars] Still, that’s a [nice?] one. Still, that’s a funny one, right? And then after that, we do with Kenny. He plays great strings, you know, with synthesizer. But it’s not [imitates] the string sound. I Love You Porgy. [plays a few bars] Et cetera. And then, Summertime. I have to [inaudible] for Gershwin, you know. [plays a few bars] Then, then we would go to a Norwegian… [laughs] uh, Brazilian song. But not so popular. It’s called The Dolphin. Stan Getz made a nice record of that on the iPhone… on the YouTube. I have it. [plays a few bars] Yeah. Then maybe another Jobim. And then what do I do? I don’t know. You know? That’s [solely?]… So if you get a hardcore today player, you know, they, they’re not… they wouldn’t get the kind of feelings sometimes I’m after, you know. I don’t want to burn all the time, you know. I want, “Yay, nice lady. How are ya doin’?” you know, whatever.
Do you keep Sophisticated Lady in your repertoire?
And then… then, of course Bluesette, you know. [plays a few notes] And then… or… [plays a few notes] I played that at the… three years ago at the Avery Fisher. No, where was it where we played?
For the NEA?
NEA. [inaudible]
It would have probably…

It was murder. Lee Konitz said, right after, he’s… “How am I gonna follow that?” [laughs] Something like that, but it was funny and nice, you know. You know? But I have a variety, you know. And then I play ‘Round Midnight all alone, [for instance?]. I did that in Antwerp. For instance, we had with Kenny, Oscar and [Iyuto?] and me. Yeah, that’s it. [laughs] And then, we… that was nice. And of course, they’re a [inaudible], but in the middle, I feature the guys, you know. Oscar sang something—one of those Brazilian showstoppers. Iyuto… [imitates]. You know? And then I’m ‘Round Midnight. You know? And then we… So, I am not quite sure, you know. And I cannot… I’m… it’s not easy to get, you know, and with those musicians, they play my stuff and it comes out okay. And they are good musicians, too, you know. Anyway, that’s it.
Well, one of the… when I go to YouTube and I put in Toots Thielemans, one of the first clips that comes up is with you and Stevie Wonder playing, of course, Bluesette.
Yeah.
And you’re starred and then he comes out from the audience…
Yeah.
‘Cause you quote, “You are the sunshine of my life,” and then he comes out. [laughs]
Yeah. Yes.
And you talk about that event?

Well, of course. For me, Stevie is… I, and I certainly cannot… I can’t play the notes maybe that he played, but [that their?] thing [that?] you guys got and some other guys tried to get… [laughs] But he’s fantastic. And he’s a human being, too, you know. One day… it must be twenty years ago, I think… he played a concert in Brussels, and we went to hear him. And he knew. I think that somehow it got to him that I was in the audience. And he said, and he put a little quote, you know, “Yeah, Toots knows that thing,” or something like that, you know. Or [inaudible]. I think he had one of those songs: I Know the Way… “And Toots knows the way, too,” you know. Something like that, you know. And then we wound up going for dinner in a restaurant in Brussels. And at one… he asked me, “Toots, what’s your day of birth date?” And because he’s Black Bull Music, too.
Right. He’s a Taurus.
[inaudible/overlapping voices]
Taurus. Yeah. Black Bull Music.
Taurus, or something like [that?].
Right, yeah.

“Oh, I was born… I’m a Taurus.” “Yeah? Well, maybe I’m black bull but you sure are white bull.” I mean, that’s… Stevie said that at a table there. And we were… a couple of years ago, we were playing at the… in Holland at the North Sea Festival. And I had made the record with strings or something. And while… excuse me. Our performance was finished, and my manager who passed away now, dear. He goes and clean ups and gets my stuff, and Herbie Hancock comes through, you know. And Herbie at… we had met them in… I wasn’t there. “What is this here?” “Well, that’s for Toots,” you know. “Oh, tell Toots…” [inaudible] “Stevie Wonder asked me to produce a record with Quincy and him.” A jazz record. But it never happened, you know. But that was sort of a… if not the feel, something close to it. But he’s fantastic. “Hey, Stevie. I’ll buy at hat to take off to you.” [laughs]
But it’s such a touching film clip because…
No, but, but he uses the harmonica with an octave deeper than mine.
Mm-hmm. ‘Cause I know at one point he starts the Bluesette melody. He’s way down, way down. Yeah, yeah.
Yeah, yeah.
And then at the end, you guys kiss and hug and it’s just, just beautiful.
Oh, yeah, it’s [inaudible/overlapping voices].
Yeah.
I didn’t know. Yes, of course. But I didn’t know he was in the audience.
Oh.

Not really. Or he didn’t see me. [laughs] I’m trying to be funny. Yeah. [laughs] Yeah, those blind people, you know. [laughs] No. But he… we met afterwards. But that was a, a nice award [there?]. All our music that was $100,000… Every two years or every year, they choose a jazz artist to get an award. And that was the year Stevie got it. That’s it. That’s about all I got to say. And my, my credo is “Be yourself. No more, no less.” And to be yourself is not the easiest thing. Sometimes I get… some people tell me I’m too modest, so I underestimate, or sometimes when I’m hot, I feel I overestimate myself. You have to find a way in. That’s wisdom. As you told me before, the Greek wisdom. Socrat…
Socrates.
Socrates. Bye. [plays a couple of notes]
[laughs] Toots, I just want to say thank you so very much for allowing us the time to have this talk.

And again, I’m saying, I’m hoping all those peoples I quoted, and they didn’t allow me to quote, all right? Like Bird is not here to say yes or no. [unintelligible] [laughs] He called me a [monk?] [unintelligible] Benny Goodman’s here. [laughs] But it’s true. But I… Sorry, Bird, if I, if I overstepped my welcome. [laughs]
But they’re your memories, so that…
What?
I said that’s from your memory so you share what you have.
Yeah, that’s…
That’s all we can ask.
That’s all I got, you know.
That’s all we can ask. [laughs] But again, Toots, thank you so much.
You are very welcome [inaudible/overlapping voices].
For me this has been a great, great inspiration.
And…
Ken.
Ken.
Yeah.
Hey, Ken. Ken: Thank you.
And our Belgian team.
Yes. Maybe get their names. Could you say their names on, for the camera?
Bart.
Bart, you see.
Like Simpson.
Bart. [laughs] Okay. On the camera.
And Peter.
Peter the journalist. From, from Belgian. So…
[Lombart?].
Lombart? Yeah? Lombart: Yes.
Wonderful. Okay. So we just want to say thank you. Toots, again. Just a great inspiration. For me, Toots Thielemans is like heart. He’s the heart. He’s the heart of this music.
Well…
What else can you ask for, huh? [laughs]

Say, if you… and I said once at an interview, you’ve got to live… I think after [Brusella?]… in Brussels, I played… Whatever you do, you got somehow… it’s gotta come from the heart. And if you don’t come from the heart, it’s [blows raspberry]. [unintelligible]. [laughs] You can say it’s bullshit. [laughs] But it’s just not far from that, you know. Or I mean, it’s not easy to do everything from the heart. We know that. I know that. [laughs] Okay.
Thank you, Toots.

And again, I’d like to say, more than gratitude, more than appreciation for my lady, [Hugette?]. She, she paid the dues thirty years ago. That’s when we met. Yeah, about thirty years ago. And then after a while, we were able… I had made royalties and work. And well, after fifty years, you make a little money, right? [laughs] We were able to buy this apartment here, right. And now, it is our [inaudible]. I mean, if we have to sell it, it’s [way?] but much more. But she [did it?]. You know, I only… you know, paid so many checks and things. But she got the… all the decoration. And we can turn on the-­ ###

segments.title: Opening of the Smithsonian interview with Toots Thielemans
segments.summary: Header and Anthony Brown's introduction of the August 31, 2011 session.

segments.title: His real name Jean and his April 29, 1922 birth
segments.summary: Toots gives his four first names and birth date, which he shares with Duke Ellington.

segments.title: Growing up in the Marolles, Brussels, and his parents' beer café
segments.summary: Born in Brussels in the Marolles district, where his parents ran a small beer café; he describes his Flemish, Walloon and Brussels roots.

segments.title: Learning four languages at school
segments.summary: After twelve years of school he knew French, Flemish, English and German, helped by American movies.

segments.title: Parents' work and his younger sister Mariette
segments.summary: The family labored at the café; his sister Mariette was born in 1929.

segments.title: Playing Ramona at age three and his Socialist father
segments.summary: Taken to a Ramon Novarro film at three, he came home playing the song; his father was a militant Socialist.

segments.title: Imitating the café accordionist with a shoebox
segments.summary: He mimicked the Sunday accordion player with a cardboard shoebox before getting a real accordion.

segments.title: No school music; Louis Armstrong record and discovering the harmonica
segments.summary: School had little music; he recalls buying an Armstrong record on a shop lady's advice and buying a harmonica after seeing one in a movie.

segments.title: Underground jazz fans in occupied Belgium; friend Gilbert brings a guitar
segments.summary: Under the occupation he and friends followed jazz secretly; his friend Gilbert brought a guitar to his sickbed.

segments.title: Playing Fats Waller on one string and getting hold of records
segments.summary: He proved he could play a Fats Waller tune on Gilbert's guitar and thereby became a guitarist, collecting Django Reinhardt and Lunceford records.

segments.title: Jazz as a good virus
segments.summary: Toots describes jazz as a positive contamination that catches the listener.

segments.title: Becoming a guitarist and playing for GIs after liberation
segments.summary: He studied Django records and harmony, left university, and after liberation played cafes and GI clubs with a rhythm section.

segments.title: Asthma, and the Embers in New York
segments.summary: He explains his asthma and pneumonia, then tells of visiting the Embers on his first trip, where inhaler medicine was mistaken for marijuana.

segments.chapter: Bebop and the first American trip
segments.title: Abandoning mathematics for bebop and the 1949 Paris festival
segments.summary: Back in occupation-end Belgium he commits to music, studies Gillespie and Parker records, and becomes a bebopper before playing Paris in 1949.

segments.chapter: Bebop and the first American trip
segments.title: First trip to America: Miami and Bill Gottlieb
segments.summary: On a trip with his uncle he sat in at a Miami restaurant, met photographer Bill Gottlieb, and was taken to 52nd Street.

segments.chapter: Bebop and the first American trip
segments.title: Sitting in at the Three Deuces and Billy Shaw's promise
segments.summary: He impressed Hank Jones and others with a bebop run, sat in with Tristano's group, and Billy Shaw promised to make him 'the Belgian king of bebop'.

segments.chapter: Bebop and the first American trip
segments.title: When he visited and how he learned bebop
segments.summary: He places the trip in winter, and says he learned bebop vocabulary from records and on the spot.

segments.chapter: Bebop and the first American trip
segments.title: Don Redman's orchestra: Don Byas and Billy Taylor
segments.summary: The first American musicians he saw were in Don Redman's band, including Don Byas, Peanuts Holland and Billy Taylor.

segments.chapter: Bebop and the first American trip
segments.title: Back to Europe for the Nice festival with the Belgian group
segments.summary: He rejoined the Belgian delegation for Nice, with saxophonist Bobby Jaspar.

segments.chapter: Bebop and the first American trip
segments.title: Bobby Jaspar's joke in the River Rouge men's room
segments.summary: An anecdote about Jaspar's sense of humor at a club in River Rouge when Toots was with Shearing.

segments.chapter: Bebop and the first American trip
segments.title: Members of the Belgian quintet and Armstrong missed
segments.summary: He lists the vibraphonist, Jacques Pelzer and Jaspar, and notes he did not meet Armstrong until later.

segments.chapter: Bebop and the first American trip
segments.title: Miles, Bird and the American stars at the 1949 Paris festival
segments.summary: Brown and Toots recall the lineup in Paris, including Miles Davis, Kenny Clarke and Tadd Dameron.

segments.chapter: Bebop and the first American trip
segments.title: Old jazz versus modern jazz, and being booed in Paris
segments.summary: He describes the stylistic war in France and the audience booing his harmonica and laughing at his Belgian accent.

segments.chapter: Bebop and the first American trip
segments.title: Belgian accent, language jokes and France's attitude to white jazzmen
segments.summary: He says it was only language humor, and that France long favored African American jazz over white players.

segments.chapter: Benny Goodman and first US jobs
segments.title: Meeting Bird and the Stardust record that reached Benny Goodman
segments.summary: He met Charlie Parker in Paris; his guitar-and-strings record reached Billy Shaw and Goodman.

segments.chapter: Benny Goodman and first US jobs
segments.title: The 1950 European tour with Benny Goodman
segments.summary: Goodman hired him for a European tour with Roy Eldridge, Zoot Sims and Dick Hyman, and loved his Stardust.

segments.chapter: Benny Goodman and first US jobs
segments.title: Work permit and Muriel Zuckerman's affidavit
segments.summary: Goodman tried to get him a US work permit and his secretary Muriel Zuckerman gave the affidavit.

segments.chapter: Benny Goodman and first US jobs
segments.title: Goodman tour details and learning from Dick Hyman
segments.summary: A six-week tour mostly in Italy and Scandinavia; he learned harmony from Dick Hyman and recalls Roy Eldridge.

segments.chapter: Benny Goodman and first US jobs
segments.title: Roy Eldridge, jamming and socializing after concerts
segments.summary: Eldridge wanted to jam and meet people after every concert.

segments.chapter: Benny Goodman and first US jobs
segments.title: Oslo's Bislet Stadium and Zoot Sims waiting for a solo
segments.summary: On April 29, 1950 in a cold Oslo stadium, Goodman left Zoot Sims waiting for a solo for an hour.

segments.chapter: Benny Goodman and first US jobs
segments.title: Louis Armstrong's 'Bop Chops' and his first US job with Charlie Parker
segments.summary: Armstrong greeted him as Bop Chops; his first American gig was with the Charlie Parker All-Stars on the Dinah Washington show at the Earle Theater.

segments.title: Lead-in to the Shearing story and camera glare pause
segments.summary: Toots offers to tell how he met Shearing; the crew adjusts the camera to avoid reflection.

segments.title: Tony Scott takes him backstage to audition for George Shearing
segments.summary: Tony Scott brought him to Shearing at Carnegie Hall; after Body and Soul, Shearing said learn the guitar book and the job was his.

segments.title: The Shearing group: guitar predecessors, Bill Clark, McKibbon, vibes, conga
segments.summary: Toots names the members of Shearing's quintet, Dick Garcia before him, Al McKibbon, Joe Roland and Cal Tjader, and later Armando Peraza.

segments.title: Shearing's success and Tony Scott's welcome to New York
segments.summary: Shearing's group topped the polls but was demanding to tour with; Tony Scott introduced Toots around.

segments.title: Shearing as the best available jazz job
segments.summary: Shearing did not tour Europe; Toots saw it as the best jazz job since studio work did not suit him.

segments.title: Harmony book with Shearing and Birdland bus tour stories about Lester Young
segments.summary: After the Shearing breakup, anecdotes of studying Goetschius and of all-star Birdland tours, where Lester Young spilled his bottles and complimented Toots as 'Lady Thielemans'.

segments.title: Writing Bluesette with Stephane Grappelli in Brussels
segments.summary: The melody came to him in 1962 in a Brussels University dressing room shared with Grappelli.

segments.title: Naming Bluesette in Stockholm and his popularity in Sweden
segments.summary: In Sweden he finished the song and a producer added the S to Bluette; he also describes his Swedish fluency and acting offer.

segments.title: Coltrane, Giant Steps and a missed invitation
segments.summary: Toots practiced Giant Steps and later met Coltrane at a Miles Quintet matinee in Washington.

segments.title: After Shearing: freelance work, jingles and whistling
segments.summary: After Bluesette he became New York's go-to whistler for jingles such as John Glenn and Singer, and was on staff for the Jimmy Dean show.

segments.title: The Old Spice whistle and how much jingles paid
segments.summary: The Old Spice commercial paid well; one year of whistling brought $15,000 plus Screen Actors Guild medical coverage.

segments.title: How he got the nickname Toots
segments.summary: At a Knokke audition the poster needed a name, and he became Toots without saying a word.

segments.title: Man Bites Harmonica for Riverside, 1957
segments.summary: He recalls recording with Orrin Keepnews, Kenny Drew, Art Taylor, Wilbur Ware and Pepper Adams.

segments.title: Time Out for Decca and the Columbia record
segments.summary: He discusses the 1958 Decca date with Hank Jones and Ralph Burns and his later Columbia small group.

segments.title: Doing his own management and Bluesette royalties
segments.summary: He managed himself; Jimmy Smith's Bluesette album sold 100,000 copies.

segments.title: Ladybug becomes a hit for Herb Alpert's Tijuana Brass
segments.summary: A song he wrote after Rings of Fire, for Lou Levy's company, was recorded by the Tijuana Brass and sold six million.

segments.title: Buying the Montauk house after Yonkers
segments.summary: Neighbors in Yonkers took them to Montauk, where they bought a house.

segments.title: Jimmy Dean Show staff job
segments.summary: A one-day-a-week staff job in 1961 at $250 helped him buy a car and summer house.

segments.chapter: Quincy Jones, films and harmonica heroes
segments.title: Meeting and working with Quincy Jones
segments.summary: He met Quincy at Birdland and was flown repeatedly to Hollywood for Quincy's film and Cosby sessions.

segments.chapter: Quincy Jones, films and harmonica heroes
segments.title: John Lennon and the Rickenbacker guitar
segments.summary: He played a solid body guitar with Shearing; Lennon later told him that if it was good enough for Shearing it was good enough for him.

segments.chapter: Quincy Jones, films and harmonica heroes
segments.title: Film work, including Midnight Cowboy
segments.summary: He played harmonica on film scores in New York studios, including Midnight Cowboy, though John Barry redid the record in England.

segments.chapter: Quincy Jones, films and harmonica heroes
segments.title: Larry Adler as harmonica pioneer
segments.summary: Toots praises Adler as the pioneer who made harmonica a show instrument, though not a jazz player.

segments.chapter: Quincy Jones, films and harmonica heroes
segments.title: Stevie Wonder as a harmonica player
segments.summary: He argues Stevie is underrated as a harmonica player and mentions his Giant Steps jam.

segments.chapter: Quincy Jones, films and harmonica heroes
segments.title: Quincy calls him the blackest and the blue note from Africa
segments.summary: Toots speaks of his closeness to Black musicians, Quincy's nicknames for him, and his credo about the blue note.

segments.chapter: Quincy Jones, films and harmonica heroes
segments.title: Armstrong as first blue note contact
segments.summary: A brief exchange on whether Armstrong was his first contact with the blue note.

segments.chapter: Quincy Jones, films and harmonica heroes
segments.title: Playing a Chrysler jingle with Louis Armstrong and attending his funeral
segments.summary: He was flown in to play on an Armstrong commercial and later went with the Cavett band to Armstrong's lying in state.

segments.chapter: Quincy Jones, films and harmonica heroes
segments.title: Duke Ellington encounters and Ray Nance in Brussels
segments.summary: Toots tells of meeting Ellington briefly, and of taking Ray Nance to a record store to play his Stardust record.

segments.chapter: Quincy Jones, films and harmonica heroes
segments.title: Donald Byrd, Herbie Hancock and Charlie Parker memories
segments.summary: At a 52nd Street rehearsal studio he hears Donald Byrd and finds Herbie Hancock for a Long Island gig, and recalls Parker and Byrd in Philadelphia.

segments.chapter: Second day: Montreux, Brazil, Bill Evans
segments.title: End of first day and opening of second day
segments.summary: Brown wraps up the first session and opens September 1 at Toots' New York apartment.

segments.chapter: Second day: Montreux, Brazil, Bill Evans
segments.title: Clarifying the Getaway film date with Quincy Jones
segments.summary: They identify the film as The Getaway and Toots repeats the anecdote of being called back to Hollywood.

segments.chapter: Second day: Montreux, Brazil, Bill Evans
segments.title: Montreux Jazz Festival pairings with Oscar Peterson
segments.summary: Toots recalls Claude Nobs and an unrehearsed Montreux set with Oscar Peterson, Joe Pass and Louie Bellson.

segments.chapter: Second day: Montreux, Brazil, Bill Evans
segments.title: Toots in New York with Herbie Hancock, 1968
segments.summary: He shares a modest verdict on his Herbie Hancock album.

segments.chapter: Second day: Montreux, Brazil, Bill Evans
segments.title: The roots of his love of Brazilian music
segments.summary: He explains the minor seventh chord as smile and tear and the harmonic appeal of Jobim and Bonfa.

segments.chapter: Second day: Montreux, Brazil, Bill Evans
segments.title: Elis Regina in Sweden and the Brasil Project
segments.summary: A 1972 Swedish TV session with Elis Regina led to the 1990 Brazilian albums; he later received a Brazilian honor.

segments.chapter: Second day: Montreux, Brazil, Bill Evans
segments.title: Brazilian harmony and rhythm, Ivan Lins
segments.summary: He discusses harmony and runs in Ivan Lins's songs and Brazilians knowing him from Shearing.

segments.chapter: Second day: Montreux, Brazil, Bill Evans
segments.title: Recording Affinity with Bill Evans
segments.summary: Helen Keane's call, Toots auditioning at Hoppers with the Paul Simon song, and Evans doubling his fee.

segments.chapter: Second day: Montreux, Brazil, Bill Evans
segments.title: Playing together with Evans on Affinity
segments.summary: Evans wanted him to play more; the cover and the Days of Wine and Roses interplay.

segments.title: Pianists, Dick Hyman and the Birdland bus tours
segments.summary: Toots recalls Hyman and George Shearing's six years, including the all-star bus with Basie, Billie Holiday and Lester Young.

segments.title: Interruption and recap
segments.summary: Equipment and phone interruptions before returning to bus travel.

segments.title: Lester Young and Tweedlee Dee on the bus
segments.summary: A story of everyone competing to sit next to Lester Young, who loved Tweedlee Dee.

segments.title: Traveling the South and the Ray Charles jukebox
segments.summary: Only two white guys on the bus; at stops everyone raced to the jukebox for Ray Charles.

segments.title: Shearing's vibraphonists, Johnnie Ray and Cal Tjader
segments.summary: Toots clarifies who played vibes and describes Cal Tjader's love of Milt Jackson.

segments.title: His wife and age
segments.summary: He praises his wife's support and admits musicians are hard to live with.

segments.title: Reacting to segregation in America
segments.summary: Brown asks if he was shocked by segregation; Toots says he wanted to be in Black parts of cities.

segments.title: Segregated hotels, Bill Clark's name and Joe Wilder in the pool
segments.summary: He recalls separate hotels in Washington and Baltimore, the Bill Clark correction and Joe Wilder's swim.

segments.title: Goodman and Shearing as integration pioneers
segments.summary: They discuss mixed bands and why race did not affect Toots.

segments.title: Paul Simon and Phil Ramone's Night Game session
segments.summary: He tells how Phil Ramone got him on Simon's album and about his worry that he had laid an egg.

segments.title: Members of Paul Simon's band: Steve Gadd, Hugh McCracken, Richard Tee, Sanborn
segments.summary: Toots describes the band members' playing and personalities.

segments.title: Sanborn's remark after Toots's Montreux solo
segments.summary: Sanborn followed him in Montreux and said he had left his ass on stage.

segments.title: Peggy Lee in Las Vegas
segments.summary: He played Makin' Whoopee with Peggy Lee in Las Vegas and played a Swedish song for her.

segments.title: Shirley Horn and her trio
segments.summary: Horn only sounded right with her own rhythm section.

segments.title: Drummers: Bill Clark, Steve Gadd and Elvin Jones
segments.summary: He recalls the feel with Bill Clark and Steve Gadd and a J.J. Johnson date with Elvin Jones.

segments.title: Ed Thigpen, Jimmy Cobb and Grady Tate
segments.summary: Short remarks on Thigpen's rim shot and Grady Tate telling him to play his chrome sandwich.

segments.title: A Montreux trio with Dizzy Gillespie and its drummer
segments.summary: Toots recalls a drummer he calls Mr. Soul in a Dizzy trio and meeting him again at North Sea.

segments.title: Billy Brooks and Oliver Jackson, drummers who left America
segments.summary: Brown raises drummers forgotten after moving to Europe, and Marsalis's drummer Ali Jackson.

segments.title: Kenny Clarke and Annie Ross
segments.summary: He recalls Clarke, Annie Ross and the Clarke-Boland Big Band.

segments.title: Tape change; Joey Baron, Fred Hersch and Marc Johnson in his group
segments.summary: He recalls playing Blue in Green with his quartet.

segments.title: Staying current and Bill Evans late recording
segments.summary: He says he keeps assimilating new things and recalls Evans announcing a Toots arrangement.

segments.title: Pronouncing Martial Solal and turning to Jaco
segments.summary: A name pronunciation check and then Brown introduces the Jaco Pastorius project.

segments.chapter: Jaco, honors, teaching and looking ahead
segments.title: Meeting Jaco Pastorius in Berlin, 1979
segments.summary: At a Berlin festival press conference Jaco said he wanted to do a duo with Toots.

segments.chapter: Jaco, honors, teaching and looking ahead
segments.title: Touring Japan with Jaco after his stroke
segments.summary: After a stroke, Toots went to Japan with Jaco's Word of Mouth band and was looked after by Jaco.

segments.chapter: Jaco, honors, teaching and looking ahead
segments.title: Jaco's decline and Brussels visit
segments.summary: He recalls Jaco's last European tour and his Concorde trip to Brussels.

segments.chapter: Jaco, honors, teaching and looking ahead
segments.title: Bud Powell in Paris
segments.summary: A brief sighting of Bud Powell in a Paris club.

segments.chapter: Jaco, honors, teaching and looking ahead
segments.title: Honorary doctorates in Brussels
segments.summary: Toots received joint honorary degrees from two Brussels universities in 1998.

segments.chapter: Jaco, honors, teaching and looking ahead
segments.title: Becoming a Baron and the Brazilian honor
segments.summary: He was named Baron by King Albert and received Brazil's Rio Branco order.

segments.chapter: Jaco, honors, teaching and looking ahead
segments.title: The NEA Jazz Master award, 2009
segments.summary: He recalls fellow honorees and Gerald Wilson speaking for Snooky Young.

segments.chapter: Jaco, honors, teaching and looking ahead
segments.title: Billy Taylor and the Hickory House while waiting for his union card
segments.summary: Billy Taylor presented his award and had been kind to him at the Hickory House while Toots waited for a union card.

segments.chapter: Jaco, honors, teaching and looking ahead
segments.title: Teaching and practicing chords and scales
segments.summary: Toots says he cannot teach but shows the scales and chords he practices in every key.

segments.chapter: Jaco, honors, teaching and looking ahead
segments.title: Trimming the tree and playing with taste
segments.summary: He explains that improvisers should trim their language and tell a story with fewer notes.

segments.chapter: Jaco, honors, teaching and looking ahead
segments.title: Listening to younger players
segments.summary: He praises younger musicians, among them Terri Lyne Carrington, Vijay Iyer and Rudresh Mahanthappa.

segments.chapter: Jaco, honors, teaching and looking ahead
segments.title: Current repertoire and projects
segments.summary: He outlines the set list he plays now with European rhythm sections and the NEA performance.

segments.chapter: Jaco, honors, teaching and looking ahead
segments.title: Playing Bluesette with Stevie Wonder
segments.summary: Brown asks about their video; Toots recalls Stevie's visit to Brussels and ends on his credo.

segments.title: Closing thanks
